facts.fact_text: According to the applicants, in the period from 20 May to 6 July 2010 they participated in protest activities against a road-construction project in Gorky Park (Парк ім. Горького) in Kharkiv.
According to the applicants, the protest activities in Gorky Park included obstructing tree-felling work.
Tree felling commenced on 20 May 2010 in Gorky Park, attracting a number of individuals who protested against it, including, according to the applicants, the applicants themselves.
According to the applicants, there were hundreds of protesters at Gorky Park.
No formal notification of the protest had been sent to the municipal authorities.
The protesters alleged, inter alia, that the tree felling in Gorky Park was unjustified and not duly authorised, and demanded proof of its legality.
Some protesters actively attempted to interfere with the tree-felling work in Gorky Park by climbing trees with the help of climbing equipment and attaching themselves to the trees to be felled.
Some protesters interfered with work to be carried out by machinery by placing themselves in front of it.

The applicants submitted to the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court that on the morning of 28 May 2010 they had been in Gorky Park along with some other protesters to express their dissatisfaction with the tree felling.
The applicants submitted that the construction site had no boundary markers and they had believed that they were lawfully in a public open space.
At the hearing on 7 July 2010 the sixth applicant acknowledged that he had been sitting on the ground in the construction area, protesting against the tree felling, which he considered unlawful.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly define an assembly as the intentional and temporary presence of a number of individuals in a public place for a common expressive purpose, and state that all types of peaceful assembly deserve protection.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly state that the term 'peaceful' should be interpreted to include conduct that may annoy or give offence to persons opposed to the ideas being promoted, and even conduct that temporarily hinders, impedes or obstructs the activities of third parties, and that assemblies involving purely passive resistance should be characterized as peaceful.

One issue raised in connection with the Gorky Park events is whether the arrest and conviction of the first six applicants for refusal to obey orders to leave the construction site breached their freedom of peaceful assembly.
According to the Government's submissions, in response to the protesters' actions the security guards attempted to drive them away by pushing them back beyond the boundaries of the construction area.
In some instances, clashes took place between security guards and protesters in Gorky Park.
The police officers deployed at the Gorky Park construction site allegedly remained largely passive in the face of the clashes between security guards and protesters.

Material for 25 May 2010 shows a large number of police officers standing in lines blocking protesters' access to certain areas where tree felling is ongoing, or pulling individual protesters away from the trees while protesters attempt to cling to them.
Material for 25 May 2010 shows protesters being pushed, pulled and escorted away from the felling area and released.
On 28 May 2010 the first to fifth, the eighth and the tenth applicants, among other protesters, were arrested and taken to a police station.

At the police station on 28 May 2010, charges of malicious insubordination in the face of lawful demands of a police officer were drawn up against the first to fifth, the eighth and the tenth applicants.

According to the offence reports drawn up on 28 May 2010, the arrested applicants had repeatedly refused to abide by police officers' instructions to leave the construction site and resisted the officers' efforts to remove them, in particular by dragging their feet and attempting to break free and to remain on the site.
It appears that the first to fifth, the eighth and the tenth applicants were released shortly after the offence reports had been drawn up on 28 May 2010.
On various dates the offence reports drawn up on 28 May 2010 against the arrested applicants were examined by the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court.
During the hearings before the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court, the applicants pleaded not guilty.

The applicants submitted that police officers had then approached and, instead of responding to the protesters' cries for help, had taken some of the protesters, including the applicants, out of the crowd one by one and escorted them to the police station, without any demands or explanations.
At the close of the hearing on 9 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court convicted the first and second applicants as charged and sentenced them to fifteen days' administrative detention.
The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court's decision convicting the first and second applicants was enforced immediately and the applicants were taken into custody.
On 18 June 2010 the Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal upheld the conviction of the first and second applicants.
The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal reduced the first and second applicants' sentence from fifteen days to nine days' detention.
On 6 July 2010 the sixth applicant was arrested and charged with malicious insubordination in the face of orders given by police officers to leave the construction site in Gorky Park.
On 7 July 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court convicted the sixth applicant as charged and sentenced him to ten days' administrative detention.
The sixth applicant started to serve his sentence immediately after the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court's judgment of 7 July 2010.

Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that citizens have the right to assemble peacefully without arms and to hold meetings, rallies, processions and demonstrations, upon notifying in advance the bodies of executive power or bodies of local self-government.

Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that restrictions on the exercise of the right to peaceful assembly may be established by a court in accordance with the law and only in the interests of national security and public order, with the purpose of preventing disturbances or crimes, protecting the health of the population, or protecting the rights and freedoms of other persons.

In its decision of 19 April 2001 the Constitutional Court of Ukraine provided an official interpretation of Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine, in response to an application for abstract interpretation lodged by the Ministry of the Interior.

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine stated in its decision of 19 April 2001 that deadlines for advance notification of meetings, rallies, marches and demonstrations must be reasonable, and that during the advance notification period the authorities have to take preparatory actions to ensure that there are no obstacles to the event and to maintain public order and the rights and freedoms of others.

The Constitutional Court of Ukraine stated in its decision of 19 April 2001 that the period of advance notification must be sufficient for executive or local government authorities to determine whether holding such events complies with the law and, if necessary, to apply to a court under paragraph 2 of Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine to resolve any matters in dispute.

Article 185 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984 provides that malicious disobedience in the face of a lawful order or demand by a police officer who is carrying out his official duties shall be punished by a fine of between 136 and 255 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH), or by withholding 20% of earnings; or, in the event that in the particular circumstances of the case and with regard to the offender's character these measures are found to be insufficient, by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

Article 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984 provides that a breach of the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations shall be punishable by a reprimand or by a fine, and that the same actions committed within a year of the application of administrative penalties or by the organiser shall be punishable by a fine, or by correctional labour of one to two months with a deduction of 20% of earnings, or by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

Under Article 294 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984, the parties to administrative-offence proceedings have the right to appeal against court judgments within ten days of their delivery, and such an appeal is to be submitted through the court of first instance.

Under Article 294 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984, the court of first instance must, within three days, refer the appeal together with the case file to a court of appeal, which has twenty days to examine the case.

Under Article 294 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984, the court of appeal must notify the parties about the hearing not later than three days before the hearing, and the failure of parties to appear does not prevent the court from examining the case, except where a good reason is shown for their failure to appear or the court has no information that the party failing to appear has been duly notified.

Under Article 294 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984, the appellate court's examination is limited to matters raised in the appeal, unless the court discovers another breach of substantive or procedural law, and the court has the power to examine new evidence if a good reason has been shown for non-production of such evidence before the first-instance court or the first-instance court rejected such evidence without sufficient grounds.

Under Article 294 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984, the court of appeal has powers to reject the appeal, to quash the first-instance court's judgment and discontinue the proceedings or quash the judgment and adopt a new judgment, or to amend the judgment, but cannot impose a sentence more severe than that imposed at first instance, and the appellate court's decision is final and not amenable to any further appeal.
Rule 1.16 of Construction Norms and Rules III-4-80 prohibited access of unauthorised persons to construction sites.

The Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council's letter of 19 May 2010 asked the chief of the Kharkiv city police to dispatch police officers to the construction site as from 20 May 2010 to ensure public order.
On 19 May 2010 Kharkiv city police approved an action plan for ensuring public safety during the tree-felling work in Gorky Park.
According to the Kharkiv city police action plan of 19 May 2010, twenty-seven active officers were assigned for ensuring public order and safety at the construction site daily from 20 May 2010.

The Kharkiv city police action plan of 19 May 2010 mentioned that the tree felling could potentially generate picketing, demonstrations and other unexpected action by opponents of the construction project.

According to the offence reports drawn up on 28 May 2010, the arrested applicants had repeatedly refused to abide by police officers' instructions to leave the construction site and resisted the officers' efforts to remove them, in particular by dragging their feet and attempting to break free and to remain on the site.

Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that restrictions on the exercise of the right to peaceful assembly may be established by a court in accordance with the law and only in the interests of national security and public order, with the purpose of preventing disturbances or crimes, protecting the health of the population, or protecting the rights and freedoms of other persons.

The police officers deployed at the Gorky Park construction site allegedly remained largely passive in the face of the clashes between security guards and protesters.

Material for 25 May 2010 shows a large number of police officers standing in lines blocking protesters' access to certain areas where tree felling is ongoing, or pulling individual protesters away from the trees while protesters attempt to cling to them.
Material for 25 May 2010 shows protesters being pushed, pulled and escorted away from the felling area and released.

According to the offence reports drawn up on 28 May 2010, the arrested applicants had repeatedly refused to abide by police officers' instructions to leave the construction site and resisted the officers' efforts to remove them, in particular by dragging their feet and attempting to break free and to remain on the site.
During the hearings before the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court, the applicants pleaded not guilty.

The applicants submitted to the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court that on the morning of 28 May 2010 they had been in Gorky Park along with some other protesters to express their dissatisfaction with the tree felling.
The applicants submitted that the construction site had no boundary markers and they had believed that they were lawfully in a public open space.
The applicants submitted that about 100 police officers had been standing nearby and had never asked the protesters to leave the area.
The applicants submitted that a number of men in black with Municipal Guard (MG) badges had surrounded the protesters and started pressing them into a tight circle.

The applicants submitted that police officers had then approached and, instead of responding to the protesters' cries for help, had taken some of the protesters, including the applicants, out of the crowd one by one and escorted them to the police station, without any demands or explanations.
The applicants submitted that they had followed the police officers without offering any resistance.

Video material for 28 May 2010 shows the individual in civilian clothing repeating several times 'Please leave the construction site', receiving the response 'This is a park, not a construction site'.

Video material for 28 May 2010 shows the police officer in charge exchanging inaudible words with a person who appears to be one of the surrounded protesters, appearing to say 'Do you wish to leave [the territory]?', and then saying to the other officers 'To the police station!'
Video material for 28 May 2010 shows police officers prising individuals from the group and leading them away from the marked-off area, with several seen dragging their feet and arguing.

In his statement to the police the first applicant said that at 7.30 a.m. on 28 May 2010 he had been in Gorky Park with his bicycle, had been grabbed by people with Municipal Guard (MG) badges and then handed over to the police.

In his statement to the police the second applicant said that at 7.20 a.m. on 28 May 2010 he had been in Gorky Park near the railway crossing, had seen a crowd and come closer to find out what was going on, and had been unaware that construction work was being conducted there.

The second applicant stated to the police that individuals with Municipal Guard (MG) badges had pushed him and others away from the railway crossing and encircled them, after which police officers had come and dragged him out of the circle and to the police station, and that he had not heard any warnings to leave the site.
On 28 May 2010 the cases against the first and second applicants were sent to court.
The first and second applicants requested that the hearings in their cases be postponed as they needed time to appoint a lawyer, and they appointed a lawyer on 28 May 2010.
On 9 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court held a hearing at which it heard the police officers, who supported the charges and the account of events set out in the offence reports.

At the hearing on 9 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court also heard the first and second applicants and some witnesses, and examined the video recording submitted by the applicants' lawyer.

The first applicant stated at the hearing on 9 June 2010 that on the morning of 28 May 2010 he had been cycling through Gorky Park on his way to work, had seen many people where trees were being felled and had gone closer.
The first applicant stated that there had been red-and-white tape but he had not realised that the area in question was a construction site.

The first applicant stated that people with Municipal Guard (MG) badges had tried to push him and others away from the railway crossing and had surrounded them, after which he had been taken away by police officers who had not addressed any orders to him personally.

The second applicant stated at the hearing on 9 June 2010 that on the morning of 28 May 2010 he had gone to Gorky Park to look at the events surrounding the tree felling, that there had been a lot of people there, and that there had been red-and-white tape but he had not understood that it was a construction site and that his presence there could be dangerous.
At the close of the hearing on 9 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court convicted the first and second applicants as charged and sentenced them to fifteen days' administrative detention.

The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court stated that, in view of the examined evidence including that submitted by the defence, it was convinced that the first and second applicants were guilty as charged.

The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court stated that the video recording submitted by the applicants' lawyer had not exculpated the first and second applicants since it had pauses and did not show certain witnesses, and therefore could not be regarded as a complete record of the events.

The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court stated that having examined the circumstances of the case and the character of the first and second applicants, it was convinced that a punishment less severe than detention would not be adequate.
The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court's decision convicting the first and second applicants was enforced immediately and the applicants were taken into custody.
On 10 June 2010 the first and second applicants' lawyer appealed to the Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal against the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court's judgments.

The first and second applicants' lawyer argued on appeal that the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court had failed to set out its analysis of the evidence which had led it to the conclusion that the applicants were guilty, and had thus failed adequately to reason its judgments.

The first and second applicants' lawyer argued on appeal that under the Code of Administrative Offences administrative detention could only be applied in exceptional cases, and that the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court had failed to explain the exceptional nature of the applicants' cases which would justify the severity of the punishment imposed.
On 18 June 2010 the Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal heard the appeals of the first and second applicants in their absence but in the presence of their lawyer.
On 18 June 2010 the Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal upheld the conviction of the first and second applicants.
The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal found that the case-file material showed that the police officers had acted lawfully in directing the first and second applicants to leave the construction site.
The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal found that the construction work was being conducted on the basis of valid permits and the appellants had failed to show otherwise.

The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal concluded that the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court had not had sufficient grounds to impose the maximum punishment on the first and second applicants, having failed to sufficiently take into account the circumstances of the cases and the applicants' personal characteristics.
The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal reduced the first and second applicants' sentence from fifteen days to nine days' detention.

In the course of the hearing before the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court, the third applicant stated that he had indeed been in Gorky Park, had not heard any orders to leave the site from the police officers but had heard it from a person in civilian clothing, and had been dragged from the circle by police officers who had taken him to the police station.
On 14 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court, having heard the police officers, the third and fourth applicants and some witnesses, convicted the third and fourth applicants as charged.
The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court sentenced the third applicant to a fine of 136 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH), at the time the equivalent of about 14 euros (EUR).
The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court sentenced the fourth applicant to a fine of 170 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH), at the time the equivalent of about 17 euros (EUR).

In his appeal the third applicant argued that he could not be held liable for failure to comply with the order of the police since he had had the right to be present in Gorky Park and the order to leave it had been without legal basis.
The fourth applicant argued on appeal that police officers had not issued any order to leave the construction site.
On 27 July 2010 the Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in the third applicant's case.
On 11 August 2010 the Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in the fourth applicant's case.

On 23 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court, having heard the police officers, the fifth applicant and some witnesses, convicted the fifth applicant as charged and fined him 170 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH), at the time the equivalent of about 17 euros (EUR).

On 27 July 2010 the Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal quashed the fifth applicant's conviction by a final decision and discontinued the proceedings against the fifth applicant under Article 22 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984.

The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal found that the trial court had correctly established the facts concerning the fifth applicant's guilt, but that its judgment lacked reasoning as to the degree of dangerousness of the applicant's conduct and his personal characteristics.

The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal found it established that the fifth applicant's registered residence was in Kharkiv, that he was employed and that his actions had not caused prejudice to the public interest or to individuals.

The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal found that the delinquent element in the fifth applicant's conduct had been so insignificant that an oral reprimand would have sufficed under Article 22 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984, and proceeded to issue the reprimand.
On 8 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court discontinued proceedings against the eighth applicant.
On 12 July 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court discontinued proceedings against the tenth applicant.

In its judgment concerning the eighth applicant, the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court noted that his explanations were consistent with a private video recording of the events submitted by him, and that there were inconsistencies between various police reports in the case file and a lack of evidence that the officers had duly instructed him to leave.

Concerning the tenth applicant, the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court likewise pointed to inconsistencies between various police reports in the case file and the lack of evidence that the officers had duly instructed him to leave.
On 6 July 2010 the sixth applicant was arrested and charged with malicious insubordination in the face of orders given by police officers to leave the construction site in Gorky Park.
On 7 July 2010 the sixth applicant's case was heard by the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court, at which the police officers supported the charges.
At the hearing on 7 July 2010 the sixth applicant acknowledged that he had been sitting on the ground in the construction area, protesting against the tree felling, which he considered unlawful.

The sixth applicant acknowledged that he had refused to comply with the police officers' requests to leave the construction site, to the point where they had had to drag him away by the arms with his legs dragging on the ground.
The sixth applicant admitted that he had told the police officers that he would return to the construction site as soon as he could.
Witnesses at the hearing on 7 July 2010 gave testimony to the same effect as the sixth applicant's account, with one adding that the applicant had also tried to break away from the police.
On 7 July 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court convicted the sixth applicant as charged and sentenced him to ten days' administrative detention.

In justifying the sanction imposed on the sixth applicant, the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court stated that it had taken into account the nature of the offence and its specific circumstances, the applicant's personal characteristics, the fact that he had no employment, the absence of aggravating or attenuating circumstances, and the need to re-educate the offender and to prevent new offences.

The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court considered that the use of sanctions less severe than imprisonment would be insufficient and that administrative detention needed to be imposed on the sixth applicant, but not for the maximum duration provided for in the law.
The sixth applicant started to serve his sentence immediately after the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court's judgment of 7 July 2010.

The sixth applicant's lawyer lodged an appeal against the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court's judgment, arguing that the court had failed to set out its analysis of the evidence which had led it to the conclusion that the applicant was guilty, and had thus failed adequately to reason its judgment.

The sixth applicant's lawyer argued on appeal that under the Code of Administrative Offences administrative detention could only be applied in exceptional cases, and that the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court had failed to explain the exceptional nature of the applicant's case which would justify the severity of the punishment imposed.
The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal concluded that the evidence, notably the sixth applicant's own explanations in court, fully supported the finding of the applicant's guilt.

The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal found no indication of illegality in the police order to leave the construction site, in particular because the sixth applicant had not submitted any evidence of any challenge having been lodged concerning the police actions or the Executive Committee of the Kharkiv City Council's decision of 19 May 2010 authorising the tree felling.

The police chief's report of 3 June 2010 stated that the police had invited the protesters to submit an official notification of their protest action as required by Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine, but the protesters had responded that they were not organising any assembly or action but were rather present in the park as ordinary citizens.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that the policing of assemblies must be guided by the human rights principles of legality, necessity, proportionality and non-discrimination, and that the State has a positive duty to take reasonable and appropriate measures to enable peaceful assemblies to take place without participants fearing physical violence.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly state that the term 'peaceful' should be interpreted to include conduct that may annoy or give offence to persons opposed to the ideas being promoted, and even conduct that temporarily hinders, impedes or obstructs the activities of third parties, and that assemblies involving purely passive resistance should be characterized as peaceful.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that law enforcement officers should allow time for people in a crowd to respond as individuals to the situation they face, including any warnings or directions given to them.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that if dispersal is deemed necessary, the assembly organiser and participants should be clearly and audibly informed prior to any intervention by law enforcement personnel, and should be given reasonable time to disperse voluntarily, and only if participants then fail to disperse may law enforcement officials intervene further.

Amnesty International's letter of 17 June 2010 stated that witnesses reported that at no point during the events of 28 May 2010 did the police officers make any requests or demands to the demonstrators that might have resulted in the charges against Andrei Yevarnitsky and Denis Chernega.

Amnesty International's letter of 17 June 2010 stated that Andrei Yevarnitsky and Denis Chernega appeared to have been sentenced to a punishment amounting to imprisonment for the peaceful exercise of their rights to freedom of assembly and expression, and that the organisation considered them to be prisoners of conscience.

One issue raised in connection with the Gorky Park events is whether alleged verbal and physical harassment on the part of the personnel involved in the road-construction project against all the applicants breached their right to freedom of peaceful assembly.
According to the Government's submissions, in response to the protesters' actions the security guards attempted to drive them away by pushing them back beyond the boundaries of the construction area.
In some instances, clashes took place between security guards and protesters in Gorky Park.
On at least fifteen occasions ambulances were called to the Gorky Park construction site during the protest events.
The police officers deployed at the Gorky Park construction site allegedly remained largely passive in the face of the clashes between security guards and protesters.
According to the seventh applicant, police officers who were standing nearby on 31 May 2010 observed the assault on her without reacting to her cries for help.
On 1 June 2010 the seventh applicant complained to the head of the Dzerzhinsky District police that on 31 May 2010 she had been hit in the back by Municipal Guard (MG) staff.

Video and photographic material for 31 May 2010 shows a tumultuous scene with men in black with badges confronting a large group of individuals in civilian clothing, pulling some protesters away from an area they are attempting to protect, and then forming an elbow-to-elbow line blocking access.
Video material for 31 May 2010 shows individuals in civilian clothing on the protesters' side filming the events, with shouts of 'Police!' and 'Call an ambulance!'
Video material for 31 May 2010 shows a woman (apparently the seventh applicant) lying on the ground surrounded by the crowd, after which an ambulance team arrives and takes her away.

On various dates the protesters, including some of the applicants, complained to the law-enforcement authorities that they had been assaulted by unidentified loggers and men in black clothing with Municipal Guard (MG) badges.
The protesters' complaints to law-enforcement authorities also alleged that the police officers stationed nearby had done nothing to protect them during the Gorky Park events.
The protesters' complaints were investigated by the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office.
On or around 3 June 2010 two television companies sent to the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office, at its request, their video recordings of the events in Gorky Park.

On 3 June 2010 the assistant prosecutor of Kharkiv questioned Mr Kl., director of Municipal Guard (MG), and the heads of four departments of that company about the presence and acts of the guards in the area.
Mr Kl. and the heads of four departments of Municipal Guard (MG) stated that there had been nobody from the company present in the area except them.

Mr Kl. and the heads of four departments of Municipal Guard (MG) stated that there had been a lot of men in black with MG badges who were not in fact the company's employees, and that on 28 May 2010, after having been rebuked by Mr Kl., those individuals had taken the badges off.
On 3 June 2010 the chief of the Kharkiv police sent to the Kharkiv city prosecutor a report summarising the law-enforcement measures taken in the course of the protests in Gorky Park.
The police chief's report of 3 June 2010 stated that Sh. and K., the heads of the NGOs Pechenigy and My Kharkivyany, had taken part in the protests.

The police chief's report of 3 June 2010 stated that the police had invited the protesters to submit an official notification of their protest action as required by Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine, but the protesters had responded that they were not organising any assembly or action but were rather present in the park as ordinary citizens.

The police chief's report of 3 June 2010 stated that police officers had been deployed in full force as envisaged by the law-enforcement plan, that is twenty-seven officers on site daily from 20 May to 2 June 2010, except for 23, 29 and 30 May 2010 when two officers had been deployed.
The Kharkiv city prosecutor's office questioned a number of police officers, employees of subcontractor companies, and journalists in the course of its investigation.
The Kharkiv city prosecutor's office examined video evidence of the Gorky Park events provided by the protesters.
The Kharkiv city prosecutor's office solicited information from the local hospital concerning reports of injuries sustained in the course of the events in Gorky Park.
On 17 and 18 June 2010 the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office questioned twenty employees of private security company PS.
The twenty PS employees stated that they had not assaulted the protesters, had not deployed any special gear but had indeed pushed the protesters away from the construction site.
On 24 June 2010 the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office decided not to institute any criminal proceedings.
On 4 August 2010 the Kharkiv regional prosecutor's office overruled the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office decision of 24 June 2010 not to institute criminal proceedings and ordered a further inquiry.

Following an additional round of pre-investigation enquiries, on 9 August 2010 the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office decided not to institute criminal proceedings against loggers A. and K., managers of the Main Contractor and subcontractor companies, Municipal Guard (MG), the Kharkiv City Council or its executive authorities, including the Kharkiv Municipal Construction Department, for lack of constituent elements of a crime in their actions.

The decision of 9 August 2010 stated that it was the result of an investigation conducted in response to a large number of complaints in connection with the Gorky Park events, including from several members of parliament, a member of the regional council, the Pechenigy NGO, a number of journalists and a number of protesters, including the applicants' then representative Mr Bushchenko, and the seventh and ninth applicants.

The decision of 9 August 2010 stated that in the course of the investigation more than a hundred people had been questioned, including protesters, police officers, employees of the Main Contractor and subcontractors, and Municipal Guard (MG) staff.
The Kharkiv city prosecutor's office had also examined photographs and video recordings of the Gorky Park events, including those provided by news outlets, complainants and NGOs.

The decision of 9 August 2010 described the events of 28 May 2010 as follows: at around 7 a.m. the Main Contractor's staff had marked the boundaries of the construction site with tape and Municipal Guard (MG) staff had taken up the duties of guarding it.

According to the decision of 9 August 2010, the Municipal Guard (MG) staff had asked individuals who were within the perimeter to leave the area in order to avoid the risk of trauma from the construction equipment, and when they refused, the Main Contractor's management had appealed to the police for help in removing those individuals from the construction site.
According to the decision of 9 August 2010, some protesters had then been arrested as they had refused to leave the construction site on 28 May 2010.
Private security company PS staff had provided guard services on the Gorky Park construction site from 28 May to 2 June 2010.

When questioned, the private security company PS guards stated that they had avoided any conflict with the protesters and had not assaulted them, despite provocative behaviour on the part of the latter.

The Kharkiv city prosecutor's office concluded in the decision of 9 August 2010 that no criminal-law provision had been breached in the course of issuance of approvals for the road construction project, tree removal, the construction work or interactions with the protesters.

The Kharkiv city prosecutor's office concluded in the decision of 9 August 2010 that loggers A. and K. had not committed any offence, for the reasons set out in the Government's version of the events of 2 June 2010.
On 13 August 2010 the police refused to institute criminal proceedings in connection with the seventh applicant's complaint of ill-treatment.

On 20 March 2012 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court quashed the police decision of 13 August 2010 on the grounds that the requirements of the Code of Criminal Procedure of 1960 concerning pre-investigation enquiries had not been complied with and the seventh applicant's allegations had not been verified.

The applicants submitted a copy of a letter from their lawyer to the district police dated 3 October 2014, stating that after the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court's decision of 20 March 2012, the seventh applicant had not been informed about any further progress in the proceedings.

According to the Government, the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office investigated possible official involvement in the alleged attacks on the seventh and ninth applicants and, having found no such involvement, forwarded the material to the police to investigate the possibility that bodily injuries may have been inflicted by private parties.
On 20 August 2010 the police decided not to institute criminal proceedings in respect of possible bodily injuries inflicted on the seventh and ninth applicants by private parties.

In their response of 15 November 2011 to the Government's observations, the applicants alleged that they had learned about the decision of 20 August 2010 only from those observations and had never been provided with a copy.

The applicants submitted copies of letters addressed to the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office and to the city and district police chiefs in which they had asked to be provided with a copy of the decision of 20 August 2010, and enclosed postal receipts showing that those letters had been delivered on 9 and 10 November 2010.

In their comments of 1 March 2012 concerning the applicants' observations of 15 November 2011, the Government commented on a number of factual matters raised by the applicants but not on the applicants' alleged inability to obtain a copy of the decision of 20 August 2010.

On 31 July 2014, in response to the Court's request for further observations, the Government informed the Court that material concerning enquiries into the seventh and ninth applicants' allegations of ill-treatment had been destroyed due to the expiry of the time-limit for their preservation.
The Government provided a statement documenting the destruction of the material concerning enquiries into the seventh and ninth applicants' allegations of ill-treatment, dated 9 September 2013.

In November 2010 a number of protesters, including all the applicants, lodged an action with the Kharkiv Circuit Administrative Court, complaining that the police had failed to protect them against assaults during their peaceful protest against the tree felling, in particular on 28 and 31 May and 1 and 2 June 2010.

According to the Government, in the course of the trial before the Kharkiv Circuit Administrative Court, the seventh applicant was examined by a representative of the police and stated that she could not say with certitude who had hit her on 31 May 2010 and only supposed that it had been a person in black.
On 24 May 2011 the Kharkiv Circuit Administrative Court rejected the applicants' claim that the police had failed to protect them against assaults during their protest.
On 9 December 2011 the Kharkiv Administrative Court of Appeal upheld the Kharkiv Circuit Administrative Court's decision of 24 May 2011.

On 26 June 2014 the High Administrative Court allowed an appeal lodged by the applicants and remitted the case to the Kharkiv Circuit Administrative Court for re-examination on the grounds that the lower courts' examination of the facts had been incomplete.

The High Administrative Court found that the lower courts had failed, in particular, to establish whether attacks on the protesters had really taken place, the list of the officers present, and whether the protesters had appealed for help.

As of 8 October 2014, the date of the last communication from the applicants on this point, the applicants' claim concerning the police's failure to protect them was pending before the Kharkiv Circuit Administrative Court.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that the policing of assemblies must be guided by the human rights principles of legality, necessity, proportionality and non-discrimination, and that the State has a positive duty to take reasonable and appropriate measures to enable peaceful assemblies to take place without participants fearing physical violence.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that law enforcement officials must protect participants of a peaceful assembly from any person or group that attempts to disrupt or inhibit it in any way.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that law-enforcement officials should be liable for any failure to fulfil their positive obligations to protect and facilitate the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, and that liability should also extend to private agencies or individuals acting on behalf of the state.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that if the force used is not authorized by law or more force was used than necessary, law-enforcement officers should face civil and/or criminal liability, as well as disciplinary action, and that relevant law-enforcement personnel should also be held liable for failing to intervene where such intervention may have prevented other officers from using excessive force.

The United Nations Special Rapporteurs' joint report A/HRC/31/66 stated that civilian private security services should not perform policing-type functions in relation to assemblies, but where this occurs, such services must respect and protect human rights and should comply with the highest voluntary standards of conduct.

In his report on the right to life and the use of force by private security providers in law-enforcement contexts issued in 2016 (A/HRC/32/39), the United Nations Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions stated that where States choose to devolve some of their responsibilities for the provision of security to private entities, those actions are attributable to the State, and at least the same restrictions apply to private security providers operating in such a context as would apply to State law enforcement personnel.

The United Nations Special Rapporteur's report A/HRC/32/39 stated that the responsibility to plan an appropriate operational response to an emerging situation applies as clearly to private security providers as it does to State law enforcement, and that in the case of private security providers there exists an additional potential precautionary step, namely to call upon the State's law enforcement personnel.

The United Nations Special Rapporteur's report A/HRC/32/39 stated that in circumstances where private security providers resort to force having turned down an opportunity to defer to the State's police, their full compliance with the requirements of precaution would be called into question.

The United Nations Special Rapporteur's report A/HRC/32/39 stated that in contexts such as mass labour protests or disputes or other mass gatherings taking place on or around private property, the police should be called in whenever uncertainties exist with regard to private and public interests, especially concerning the use of force.

The United Nations Special Rapporteur's report A/HRC/32/39 stated that States must impose on private security providers and their personnel a duty of precaution concerning recruitment, training, equipment, planning, command and control, and reporting, and that in circumstances likely to require the use of force, private security personnel have a responsibility to inform State law enforcement and to follow any instructions given.
